title: Cascading 3D Reconstruction Procedure of Composite Structures from Microtomography Data
author: Kabbej, Guillard, et al.

steps.title: Extract cuboid samples from tomogram
steps.instruction: From the 3‑D grayscale micro‑tomography image (resolution 0.65 µm³/voxel, overall size 1844 × 1403 × 298 µm³) extract twelve cuboid sub‑volumes of equal height 250 µm from different zones (exact lateral dimensions are listed in Table S1.1). Each sub‑volume will be analysed separately (≈10–15 min per sample, ≈3 h total) on a Dell workstation (Intel Xeon E‑2176 M 2.7 GHz, 32 GB RAM).

steps.title: Binarize samples and select threshold
steps.instruction: Open each cuboid in ImageJ, use the “3D Objects Counter” plugin to convert the grayscale data to a binary image (matrix = 0, filler = 1). Test several threshold values on all twelve samples; compute the particle volume fraction for each threshold and compare to the known experimental filler fraction φp = 2.96 % v/v. Choose threshold 105, which yields a calculated volume fraction matching the experimental value.

steps.title: Remove edge and tiny particles
steps.instruction: From the binary data discard any particle intersecting the sample edges and any particle whose voxel count is < 30 voxels. This reduces the particle count from 21 570 to 12 812 (40.60 % of particles removed, representing 0.47 % of the total particle volume).

steps.title: Measure ellipsoid descriptors and normalize axes
steps.instruction: Using the MorphoLibJ plugin in ImageJ, fit an ellipsoid of inertia to each of the 12 812 particles and record: (i) centroid coordinates (xc, yc, zc), (ii) raw semi‑axes a1′ > a2′ > a3′, (iii) Tait‑Bryan angles ψ, θ, φ (extrinsic x‑y‑z convention). Convert the raw axes to true‑volume axes with ai = ai′ · (Vreal/Vell)¹⁄³, where Vell = π⁄6 · a1′ · a2′ · a3′ and Vreal is the particle’s actual volume.

steps.title: Standardize orientation angle intervals
steps.instruction: MorphoLibJ returns ψ ∈ [−180°, 180°], θ ∈ [−90°, 90°], φ ∈ [−180°, 180°]. Reduce ψ and φ to the interval [0°, 180°] by applying symmetry rules so that each particle orientation is represented by a unique (ψ, θ, φ) triplet.

steps.title: Convert Tait‑Bryan angles to Euler angles
steps.instruction: Transform the standardized Tait‑Bryan angles (ψ, θ, φ) into the Euler angles (γ, β, α) required by COMSOL (z‑x‑z extrinsic convention) using the conversion formulas supplied in Supplementary Section S2 (also listed in Table 1 of reference [1]).

steps.title: Fit Kernel distributions to particle descriptors
steps.instruction: In MATLAB, fit a non‑parametric truncated Kernel distribution to each descriptor: the largest axis a1, the axis ratios a1⁄a2 and a2⁄a3, and the three orientation angles ψ, θ, φ. For the ratio a1⁄a2, use four separate Kernel distributions defined over four a1 zones: a1 ≤ 20 µm; 20 µm < a1 ≤ 40 µm; 40 µm < a1 ≤ ? (next zone); a1 > ? (final zone). The fitted distributions reproduce the experimental correlations between a1, a2 and a3.

steps.title: Generate synthetic microstructures in MATLAB
steps.instruction: Run the MATLAB code (based on Tschopp’s algorithm) that populates a periodic representative volume element (RVE) with non‑overlapping ellipsoidal particles. Input the Kernel‑derived distributions, the target filler volume fraction φp = 2.96 % v/v, and the RVE size 50 × 50 × 100 µm³. Produce approximately ten independent microstructures. The code can also handle bi‑phasic or tri‑phasic systems by adding a third compartment around the particles.

steps.title: Optional: higher‑volume or spherical structures
steps.instruction: If required, repeat the generation step with a higher filler volume fraction (up to 19.91 % v/v) or replace ellipsoids by size‑heterogeneous spheres (using the equivalent‑sphere diameter distribution fitted with the same truncated Kernel law).
